newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy aims for "aggressive" sale of ENI - MD.
newsitem.headline: Italy aims for "aggressive" sale of ENI - MD.

text.p: Italy's government intends to push on with its privatisation of energy giant ENI in a "very aggressive" manner, but the placement of a third tranche will depend above all on market conditions, ENI managing director Franco Bernabe said.
He said in an interview with Nightly Business Report broadcast on Reuters Financial Television that the group was looking for growth in hydrocarbon output of four to five percent in the coming years.
The Italian Treasury has just sold off a second tranche of some 15 percent of shares in the group in an operation it described as a great success.
The Treasury now holds a stake of some 70 percent in ENI.

Asked if the government aimed to bring this down to 50 percent or even to zero, Bernabe said, "The government has not made a formal declaration, but the intention of the government is to pursue very aggressively the privatisation of ENI."
The Treasury placed an initial 15 percent of ENI stock on the market in November 1995.

As for a third tranche sale, "The Treasury...will carefully analyze the market situation to decide what to do after the (nine-month) lockout period," Bernabe said, adding the decision would be determined on the basis of market conditions.

"We are planning to increase quite aggressively the rate of growth in production and in research. We are planning to increase our production in the order of 4 or 5 pct in the next few years," he said."
"We have made a big turnaround. In 1995 we were the third most profitable oil company in the world," after three to four years of restructuring.
"We are doing our best to decrease costs and increase profitability," he added.
As for the gas sector, "sources of supply will be mostly in the next three years the traditional sources - Russia, Algeria and the Northern Countries, mainly the Netherlands," he said.
"In the future, we are planning to expand the geographic scope, adding some other Northern countries, including Norway, and perhaps some other sources of supply as well".
China "is a very important country for us...we think our prospects for expanding (there) are really quite good," Bernabe added.
He was asked about relations with Libya, where ENI is the major foreign operator, accounting for 17 percent of the country's production in 1995.

ENI has recently signed a $3 billion gas supply deal with Libya. The deal covers the export of gas from the Libyan onshore Wafa fielod and offshore Block NC-41 and a 520-km pipeline to run between Libya and Sicily.

EU officials have said that the deal could be hit by U.S. President Bill Clinton's Iran-Libya Sanctions Act signed in August to deter new investment to the two states which Washington sees as sponsors of international terrorism.
"With Libya, we have had relations for over 30 years. There are traditional links between Italy and Libya.
"As long as whatever we do complies with international agreements, we believe we will be doing what is under the international umbrella in our relations with Libya," he said.

ENI said in its recent sale prospectus, "ENI cannot predict interpretations of, or the implementation policy of the U.S. government with respect to, the Sanctions Act. However, ENI does not believe that the Sanctions Act will have a material adverse effect on the financial condition or results of operations of ENI."
